definition: Interrogate means to question someone or something closely and thoroughly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word interrogate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know interrogate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Editors at the fact desk interrogate every statistic before it reaches print.
To ask is the gentlest form of questioning — one question, no pressure — far milder than interrogate.
To quiz someone goes further than asking, firing quick questions in a row, but it stops short of interrogate, which is systematic, sustained, and pressing.

Grill is the informal, kitchen-table word for questioning someone hard — reporters grill a coach, parents grill a curfew-breaker. Interrogate does the same relentless work in official dress: systematic, sustained, often on the record. A detective interrogates a suspect; a roommate merely grills you.

To question someone is the plain, neutral act, at any intensity — one query or fifty. Interrogate marks the far end of that scale: closely, thoroughly, at length, each answer pressed for more. All interrogating is questioning; most questioning never comes near interrogation.

When the bridge's strain gauges disagreed, the engineering team interrogated the data for a week: every sensor's history pulled, every calibration date checked, every spike matched against the maintenance calendar — until the flaw stood exposed, one gauge wired backward on installation day.
Interrogate earns its force here: the data was not skimmed but pressed with question after question, systematically, until it gave up its answer.
Examine would be gentler; grill is for people under pressure; interrogate suits a thorough, relentless questioning of anything — a person, a dataset, or an account.
Interrogate is questioning at full pressure — systematic, sustained, often official.
It points outward at a person, a dataset, or an account; scrutinize, its neighbor in this unit, does the same relentless work with the eyes instead of with questions.

The painting arrived with a tidy story: a minor Dutch master, a single family's attic, four centuries of quiet.
Authenticators are paid to believe none of it politely.
For three weeks the lab interrogated the panel itself -- tree-ring dating on the oak, X-rays under the varnish, pigment scrapings no bigger than a comma.
Each test was a question put to the object, and each answer was pushed further.
The rings said the tree fell in 1650; fine, then why did one pigment not exist before 1710?
The attic story survived every round but that one.
What the seller called an heirloom, the report called, more carefully, 'a later hand on an older panel' -- a verdict no polite glance could have reached.
